title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
hookLine: Martha is busy and cross; Mary sits at his feet; one thing is needed

lines: ONE AT THE SINK, ONE ON THE FLOOR.
cards: Luke tells this story in five verses, straight after the good Samaritan. Yesterday's hero stopped and did something. Today, a guest arrives in a village, and the person doing everything gets a gentle word.
A woman named Martha received him into her house: her house, her welcome, her guest. Luke only says there was much serving; it isn't hard to imagine bread to bake and water to carry.
Her sister Mary is sitting on the floor, listening. Anyone who has been the one at the sink while others laugh in the next room may recognize Martha.

teach.b: In the King James Bible, Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." That's the place of a student; Paul later says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel.
Mary takes that place, one some readers think was usually kept for men, and nobody sends her back to the kitchen. Martha "was cumbered about much serving."

Luke's Greek word has the sense of being pulled around, drawn in every direction. Finally she comes in: "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me."
She doesn't speak to Mary; she goes over her head. The answer is gentle.

He says her name twice, the way you do with someone you love: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."
Careful here means full of care, anxious. He doesn't tell Martha to stop cooking or call serving wrong; one story earlier, the Samaritan was all service.
What he names is the worry, the many things crowding out the one. Christians read the sisters in more than one way.
Some early writers saw two callings, the active life and the quiet life of prayer, and monasteries tried to keep both.

Others say every person has a Martha and a Mary inside. And Martha gets her own great moment later: in John's Gospel, she tells Jesus plainly that she believes he is the Christ. Nobody here is the villain.
One sister just needed to sit down first.

how: Some Christians keep a short time of quiet prayer or Bible reading before the day's work begins, and in monastic communities, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican, the day is shaped by set hours of prayer between hours of work.

o: the woman who poured oil on Jesus' feet
the sister who served, pulled in every direction
the sister who sat at Jesus' feet to listen

games.q: what's inside Luke 10:38–42 — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus tells Martha that serving is wrong
he names her worry, not her work. one story earlier, the Samaritan's service is the example to follow.
sitting at a teacher's feet was the place of a student
Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel.
in John's Gospel, Martha says she believes Jesus is the Christ
John 11:27: "I believe that thou art the Christ."

games.q: you're Martha. the house is full, the bread isn't baked, and your sister is sitting on the floor. what do you do?
o: ask the guest to tell her to help.
games.why: she says: "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone?" he answers gently, saying her name twice.

practice: Before the next thing on your list, sit down the way Mary did, as if someone worth listening to were in the room, and name two or three of the many things pulling at you. Set each one down.
If you pray, simply listen without asking for anything; if you don't, listen to the quiet, to your breath, to whatever is actually here.

wordCard.voice: Martha. The sister who welcomed Jesus into her home and was pulled in every direction by much serving, while Mary sat at his feet and listened.

orig.note: Greek: she was pulled around, distracted. Luke's word for Martha with much serving; the King James Bible says cumbered.

carryVoice: Your line: one thing is needful. The worry, not the work. Day five hundred forty-two, done.
